source.title: Interference Beyond Geometry in Concept Extraction

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper measures feature geometry together with co-activation and magnitude, and reports how architecture and sparsity affect the resulting interference. It refines the claim by finding selective orthogonalization in constrained SAEs but constructive interactions when architectural constraints are relaxed; it also reports no universal scaling trend for net interference. Its cross-seed dictionary comparisons bear on the stability component of V5.
record.gate_note: Rows cover the paper's own interference measurements and cross-seed dictionary-agreement measurements. Cited findings from other work are excluded. The paper extracts SAE features from language-model activations but does not test whether those features are complete units of the underlying LLM representation or how the LLM itself distributes features across neurons.
record.test_reason: The paper's own cross-seed comparison (Appendix I, Table 1) measures whether SAE dictionaries trained on Pythia-160M activations are stable across seeds. The authors report that they differ substantially, which bears on the stability part of V5. The main interference experiments measure how SAE extractor architecture shapes decoder geometry and code statistics. That is a property of the dictionary-learning method, not a test of toy-model superposition (V1). Those results belong under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is correct. The authors additionally state that the cross-seed dictionaries differ substantially even though aggregate interference patterns are stable. The ethics section urges cautious interpretation of individual SAE features, since their separability depends on architectural choices.
record.recipe_differences: This is not a reproduction of the original toy-model method: it develops an effective-interference measure and studies learned SAEs on model activations, varying architecture and measuring co-activation-weighted geometry rather than reproducing the original toy-network setup.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported interference patterns vary with SAE architecture and with support size k and dictionary width p. The paper also reports that dictionaries differ across training seeds even when aggregate interference patterns are stable.

fits_no_version.finding: SAE interference regimes depend on extractor architecture. Tied, normalized, bias-free SAEs selectively orthogonalize co-active pairs, while global overlap rises. Bias, gain or untying retain constructive interference: total signed interference is 40–50% of reconstruction energy, net 15–25% when untied. The pattern also holds on MNIST and in SAEBench SAEs (Gemma-2-2B, Pythia).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The geometry and interference of SAE-extracted features are shaped by the extractor's architecture (tying, bias, gain), not only by the underlying representation.

record.problems: The orthogonalization theory is local to fixed supports and approximates code optimality; the authors note measured code-optimality gaps remain nonzero. The two-feature gradient result does not establish global convergence or cover support transitions. Most interference results are presented in figures without numerical values in the text, and all experiments use SAE-extracted representations rather than direct tests of the original toy-model claim. The cross-seed comparison is limited to the main runs and does not establish feature completeness or canonicality.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant reported results were left out. Figure-only trends are retained where the text explicitly states their direction or interpretation.

untested.parts: No toy model with known sparse features, no sparsity-dependent transition, no feature-importance variation, and no geometry of the network's own representation. Only extractor (SAE) geometry is studied.
Neuron polysemanticity and capacity allocation are not studied.
Origins of polysemantic neurons are not studied.
Does not test whether the LLM spreads features over neurons or whether SAEs recover the model's true features.

Completeness, canonicality across extractors or architectures (feature identity across variants is not compared), and stability across recipes are untested. Only cross-seed agreement in one setup is tested.
One-dimensional versus multi-dimensional features are not compared.

missing.what: Generality checks: interference patterns in SAEs trained on MNIST, and in independently trained SAEBench SAEs on Gemma-2-2B L12 and Pythia-160M L8. These are figure-only and bear on the fits_no_version finding, not on a version.

record.verdict_notes: The reader linked the interference rows to V1. I relinked them to none, because they characterize the SAE extractor, not superposition in a model with known sparse features. The only version-bearing result is the cross-seed agreement table, a side analysis with 3 seeds. The architecture variant used for the Figure 2 runs is not stated. The study is not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test the original toy-model setup or a general transition as feature count exceeds dimension; it does not establish a universal regular geometry or vary feature importance. The sparsity/width sweep is illustrative and the largest tied configurations are interpreted cautiously.
Does not test neuron polysemanticity or whether feature importance determines dedicated versus shared dimensions.
Does not test whether polysemantic neurons arise without capacity pressure.

Although it analyzes SAEs trained on language-model activations, it measures interactions among extracted SAE features, not feature distribution across the LLM's neurons or recovery of the LLM's underlying features.
Tests cross-seed dictionary agreement for the main runs, but not feature completeness, canonicality across extractors, or stability across training recipes generally.
Treats concepts as directions and does not compare one-dimensional features with multidimensional features.

rows.subject: Pythia-160M-deduped SAEs (TopK, JumpReLU, BatchTopK, Matryoshka; aggregate across families)
rows.stage_stated: SAEs trained on layer 8 residual-stream activations; training step varies
rows.operation_detail: Tracked global squared geometric overlap during SAE training.
rows.uncertainty: Three seeds are averaged; no error bar or other uncertainty is stated.
rows.note: The text explicitly describes the direction of change across SAE families; no plotted values are transcribed.
rows.check: Measures the training dynamics of an SAE extractor's global decoder overlap. This is not superposition in a small network with known sparse features, and V1's sparsity transition and geometry are not measurable here. Relinked to none.

rows.stage_stated: SAEs trained on layer 8 residual-stream activations; training step varies
rows.operation_detail: Tracked squared effective interference during SAE training.
rows.value: Falls from its peak during training.

rows.note: The authors interpret the divergence from global geometric overlap as selective reduction of realized interactions, not global dictionary orthogonalization.
rows.check: SAE effective interference over training is a property of the extractor, not a V1 toy-model measure. Relinked to none.

rows.subject: Pythia-160M-deduped SAEs (TopK, JumpReLU, BatchTopK, Matryoshka; aggregate across families)
rows.stage_stated: SAEs trained on layer 8 residual-stream activations
rows.operation_detail: Compared decoder orientation with co-activation-weighted feature magnitude across architectural variants.

conditions.value: co-active feature pairs; especially pairs with large πij Mij

rows.measure: Decoder orientation ρij conditional on co-activation-weighted magnitude πij Mij
rows.value: Pairs with large πij Mij concentrate near ρij = 0 or shift toward negative orientations.
rows.note: The text reports this pattern for the tied, normalized, bias-free setting across SAE families.
rows.check: Tied-SAE selective orthogonalization of co-active decoder pairs bears on SAE architecture, not on whether a network stores sparse features as nearly orthogonal directions. Relinked to none.

rows.subject: Pythia-160M-deduped SAEs (TopK, JumpReLU, BatchTopK, Matryoshka; aggregate across families)
rows.stage_stated: SAEs trained on layer 8 residual-stream activations
rows.operation_detail: Compared decoder orientation with co-activation-weighted feature magnitude after relaxing architectural constraints.

conditions.value: bias, encoder-gain freedom, or untied encoder
co-active feature pairs, including pairs with large πij Mij

rows.measure: Decoder orientation ρij conditional on co-activation-weighted magnitude πij Mij
rows.value: Pairs with large πij Mij extend toward positive ρij; the text reports this pattern for the relaxed variants.
rows.note: The paper says this pattern recurs across other SAE families; intermediate variants are not strictly ordered.
rows.check: Architecture-dependent positive decoder alignment in SAEs is not a V1 measure. Relinked to none.

rows.subject: Pythia-160M-deduped SAEs (TopK, JumpReLU, BatchTopK, Matryoshka; aggregate across families)
rows.stage_stated: SAEs trained on layer 8 residual-stream activations
rows.operation_detail: Compared positive, negative, and net normalized effective-interference contributions across architectures.
rows.baseline: Tied baseline is the reference; the text gives the untied contribution and describes the shift relative to tied.
rows.value: I+ + |I−| accounts for roughly 40–50% of reconstruction energy; the net contribution is approximately 15–25%. Untying produces the largest constructive contribution across all four families.
rows.note: The substantial positive and negative terms can partly cancel; these percentages are reported for the untied setting.
rows.check: Signed interference shares of SAE reconstruction energy are not a V1 measure. Relinked to none. Values (40–50% and 15–25%, untied) are correctly transcribed.

rows.subject: Pythia-160M TopK SAEs
rows.operation_detail: Varied support size k at fixed dictionary width and measured co-activation, conditional magnitude, overlap, and net interference.

conditions.value: biased, gain-adaptive, and untied variants for the reported overlap trend

rows.measure: Mean co-activation frequency πij; mean conditional magnitude Mij; mean absolute decoder overlap |ρij|; net interference Inet
rows.value: Increasing k raises mean πij and lowers mean Mij; mean |ρij| generally decreases in biased, gain-adaptive, and untied variants. Inet has no universal monotonic trend.
rows.note: The text calls this an illustrative diagnostic and does not assert a universal scaling law; the largest tied configurations have elevated FVU and are treated cautiously.
rows.check: The k sweep in TopK SAEs is an illustrative extractor diagnostic, not a feature-sparsity sweep in a toy model. The authors disclaim any scaling law. Relinked to none.

rows.subject: Pythia-160M TopK SAEs
rows.operation_detail: Varied dictionary width p at fixed support size k and measured co-activation, conditional magnitude, and overlap.
rows.measure: Mean co-activation frequency πij, conditional magnitude Mij, and mean absolute decoder overlap |ρij|
rows.value: Increasing p spreads co-activation across more pairs and reduces πij, while Mij and |ρij| change less in most settings.
rows.note: The paper presents this as an illustrative profile, not a universal scaling law.
rows.check: The p sweep in TopK SAEs is an extractor diagnostic, not a V1 test. Relinked to none.

rows.subject: JumpReLU SAE on Pythia-160M-deduped activations
rows.stage_stated: Three independently initialized and ordered training runs; 200M tokens
rows.operation_detail: Compared dictionaries across seed pairs using feature-matching cosine agreement.
rows.measure: Cross-seed dictionary agreement: MMCS; median; MMCS absolute-value counterpart; fraction above 0.9; fraction above 0.7
rows.uncertainty: Averaged over three seed pairs; no additional uncertainty stated.
rows.note: The authors say the learned dictionaries differ substantially despite stable aggregate interference patterns across seeds.
rows.check: Linkage and values are correct. The architecture variant (tied, untied, etc.) of the Figure 2 runs is not specified in the record. Comparison covers only 3 seeds of one setup. JumpReLU has the highest agreement (61.1% of features above 0.7).
